entry.title: Principal Component Analysis for Zero-Inflated Probability Measures via Lorenz Curves

link.title: Principal Component Analysis for Zero-Inflated Probability Measures via Lorenz Curves

entry.content: This paper develops a principal component analysis framework for probability measures associated with non-negative real-valued random variables with structural zeros. Specifically, leveraging the associated Lorenz Curve (LC) and a suitable perspective transformation of the plane, a bijective embedding is defined to treat such measures as functional data in a Hilbert space. Once the random LC is embedded in this space, standard Functional Principal Component Analysis (FPCA) becomes directly applicable, and the diffeomorphic nature of the embedding allows the main convergence results and their interpretations to be transferred back to the original space of LC. The a.s. and $L^2(\mathbb{P})$ consistency of the estimated eigenfunctions, eigenvalues, and modes of variation is subsequently investigated, both in the embedded space and, by virtue of the embedding’s diffeomorphism property, in the original LC space. Crucially, this consistency analysis accounts for the double stochasticity of the estimation problem: one level of randomness is tied to the underlying LC process itself, while the other stems from the empirical estimation of the LC from sample data. As a consequence, consistency of the Karhunen–Lo`eve reconstructions is also established, guaranteeing faithful approximation of individual curves in both spaces. Finally, the proposed FPCA methodology is illustrated on a real-world dataset of global export flows and compared with a naive FPCA approach.

entry.title: Interactive and Robust PCA Graphics with FSDA in MATLAB

link.title: Interactive and Robust PCA Graphics with FSDA in MATLAB

entry.content: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a standard method for dimension reduction and the exploratory analysis of multivariate data, but a complete applied workflow often requires more than numerical eigenvectors and static plots. This article documents a set of routines in the FSDA toolbox for MATLAB that implements an integrated workflow for interactive and robust PCA graphics. The software contribution consists of coordinating classical SVD-based PCA, dynamic biplot scaling controlled by row and column parameters, score-distance and orthogonal-distance diagnostics, hard-trimming robust PCA through the Minimum Covariance Determinant and the Forward Search, linked brushing, geographical displays, and three-dimensional projection diagnostics. The implementation returns reproducible numerical output while also exposing graphical controls for changing biplot geometry, confidence regions, displayed labels, robust trimming levels, and linked selections. The methodology is illustrated on quality-of-life indicators for Italian provinces, where the software reveals variable groups, atypical provinces, robust and non-robust PCA structures, and geographical patterns. The emphasis is on statistical software: no new PCA estimator is proposed, but established PCA and robust-PCA methodology is combined in a documented, extensible, and script-reproducible MATLAB environment.

entry.title: Maximum likelihood, neural networks and posterior mean for inferring fractional Brownian motion parameters

link.title: Maximum likelihood, neural networks and posterior mean for inferring fractional Brownian motion parameters

entry.content: Fractional Brownian motion (fBM) is a model of anomalous diffusion parameterised by a Hurst exponent $H \in (0,1)$ and a generalised diffusion coefficient $D_H > 0$. We jointly estimate $H$ and $D_H$ using maximum likelihood (MLE) from density measurements with Poisson counting noise and single-particle trajectory with Gaussian localisation error. We show that one density measurement in time cannot infer both $H$ and $D_H$ and that several time points are needed, which matters most for inference precision. For trajectories, we show that a neural network trained with a squared error loss approximates the posterior mean of $H$, which can be computed exactly at negligible cost. Paired with the profile-likelihood estimate of $D_H$, the posterior mean has the lowest root mean squared error in both $H$ and $D_H$, except near $H=0$ and $H=1$ where MLE estimates $H$ better. In vesicle trajectories from two cell types, $H$ and $D_H$ form a continuum rather than distinct modes of motion. The posterior probability that each window within a track is subdiffusive or superdiffusive shows that $26\%$ of MRC5 fibroblast and $21\%$ of HeLa vesicle trajectories contain both subdiffusive and superdiffusive windows, against $2\%$ and $7\%$ expected from estimation uncertainty alone. Intracellular cargoes therefore switch between subdiffusion and superdiffusion over time rather than forming populations with fixed $H$.

entry.title: A New Perspective on Cumulative Residual Rényi Entropy

link.title: A New Perspective on Cumulative Residual Rényi Entropy

entry.content: This paper introduces a new cumulative residual R'enyi entropy (CRRE), which addresses limitations of the existing cumulative residual R'enyi entropy. The conventional measure suffers from two primary drawbacks: its failure to converge to the cumulative residual entropy (CRE) as the order parameter approaches unity, and its lack of guaranteed positivity. Our proposed CRRE resolves these issues, offering a theoretically consistent and always nonnegative measure of uncertainty in residual lifetimes. We explore its mathematical properties, including its relationship with existing information measures. Furthermore, the concept is extended to its dynamic version, and its time-dependent characteristics are investigated. A non-parametric estimator of the proposed CRRE is developed, its almost sure convergence is established, and is validated through Monte Carlo simulation. The effectiveness of CRRE as a tool for quantifying uncertainty is confirmed through its application in chaotic theory and financial data.

entry.title: Improved Forecasting for Multivariate Time Series using GNAR models with General Inverse Distance Weights

link.title: Improved Forecasting for Multivariate Time Series using GNAR models with General Inverse Distance Weights

entry.content: Many multivariate time series arise on networks where relationships between variables depend on physical or more general distances. Standard vector autoregressive models struggle in such settings due to their quadratic parameter growth, while generalised network autoregressive (GNAR) models offer a parsimonious alternative by explicitly incorporating network structures. Existing GNAR formulations assume fixed weights, typically uniform or reciprocal distances, which may not reflect the true influence of distance in real systems. We introduce a novel model with general inverse distance weights (GNARID) that extends GNAR by introducing a tunable exponent parameter that controls the strength of distance penalisation. We establish theoretical results on the consistency and asymptotic normality of new GNARID estimators, including an extension to the setting where the number of nodes grows. We analyse the effect of misspecifying the exponent on forecasting error, which helps assess how much GNAR models could be improved by our tunable weights. Simulation studies confirm the theoretical properties and show measurable benefits from correct weight specification. Using the Brumadinho ground displacement dataset, we show that proper tuning of the weight exponent improves predictive performance, highlighting the practical value of flexible distance-based weighting in network time series models.

entry.title: MCMC Can See Can’t See

link.title: MCMC Can See Can’t See

entry.content: It is folklore that passing “convergence” diagnostics does not guarantee that a Markov chain has converged. We prove this as an impossibility for any finite checklist of diagnostics. Running more chains, longer chains, and smarter diagnostics does not avoid this impossibility in certifying convergence. Under regularity assumptions, we determine how the worst-case undetected non-convergence decays as more diagnostics are added, and how to choose diagnostics optimally. Folklore suggests that the sampler’s slowest mixing modes are the “dangerous” ones that must be monitored; we prove that the slow modes yield nearly optimal diagnostics as sampling proceeds. Given a source class, we also give an anytime-valid bound on the remaining discrepancy and show how undetected bias caps the effective sample size that a finite checklist can certify.

entry.title: Testing for Peer Effects in Heteroskedastic Fixed-Effects Panels

link.title: Testing for Peer Effects in Heteroskedastic Fixed-Effects Panels

entry.content: We study testing for peer effects in linear panel models with individual and time fixed effects when the interaction network is unspecified. We propose a quadratic-form test based on the Gram matrix of residualized peer covariates. A key difficulty is that fixed-effects removal and nuisance estimation destroy the centering of a conventional leave-diagonal-out quadratic form under conditional heteroskedasticity. We introduce a leverage adjustment that restores exact conditional centering and combine it with a residual-based variance estimator. The resulting studentized statistic is asymptotically standard normal as both panel dimensions diverge, without imposing any restriction on their relative growth rates. Under additional conditions, we establish consistency against alternatives. The null theory is further extended to covariates that are weakly dependent over time; the same studentization remains valid without an additional long-run variance estimator. Monte Carlo experiments evaluate the finite-sample size and power of the proposed test across different settings and demonstrate its favorable performance relative to the existing benchmark test. Applications to state tax competition and growth spillovers among OECD countries illustrate the practical relevance in testing for peer effects without specifying the interaction network.

entry.title: Discrete p-Fold Directional Models for Binned Orientation Data with Applications to Sand-Grain Orientations and Urban Street Networks

link.title: Discrete p-Fold Directional Models for Binned Orientation Data with Applications to Sand-Grain Orientations and Urban Street Networks

entry.content: Discrete directional data exhibiting p-fold rotational symmetry, where directions separated by integer multiples of 2{\pi}/p are equivalent, arise in various applications but are often modeled using continuous distributions. In this article, we develop two general methods for constructing distributions for such data: symmetrization and folding of discrete circular distributions, and wrapping of discrete linear distributions. Particular models arising from these constructions are studied, together with their properties and estimation methods. For axial sand-grain orientation data, the proposed models are compared with discretized continuous axial distributions, whose category probabilities require numerical integration. The proposed models attain smaller Akaike information criterion values among the models considered while allowing direct likelihood evaluation without numerical integration. The framework is also applied to binned Manhattan street-orientation data, demonstrating its applicability to higher-order rotational structures, specifically the 4-fold case.

entry.title: Predicting future insurance markets: Simulation of technology adoption paths with a Bayesian Bass model

link.title: Predicting future insurance markets: Simulation of technology adoption paths with a Bayesian Bass model

entry.content: Technological progress can give rise to new loss exposures or reduce existing risks. In either case, it strongly affects insurance companies’ existing lines of business. As the magnitude of such effects is often closely connected to the innovation’s market penetration, reliably predicting its adoption process is vital in enabling insurers to adapt their business strategy accordingly. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel combination of contributions from the domain of innovation diffusion. Our methodology generates adoption scenarios that holistically account for different sources of uncertainty, offers a structured way to incorporate expert judgment and insights from pre-existing technologies, and updates its predictions as new information on the technology’s diffusion becomes available. Its modular nature ensures that components can be easily replaced by suitable alternatives. Using publicly accessible data on privately-owned battery electric vehicles in Germany, the application of our approach for predicting changes to insurance losses and for supporting insurers’ sustainability strategies is visualized in a motor insurance case study.

entry.title: Mixed Poisson diffusion models and application to posterior sampling

link.title: Mixed Poisson diffusion models and application to posterior sampling

entry.content: Diffusion models are a powerful framework for learning complex probability distributions. While widely used diffusion models for continuous data rely on Gaussian noising processes, we instead develop diffusion models based on Poisson noise. More precisely, we introduce and study a new mathematical framework, called Mixed Poisson Diffusion Models (MPDM), with noising dynamics driven by multivariate counting processes. Our methodology is motivated by Poisson inverse problems. The success of Gaussian diffusion models has led to their use as prior models in a growing number of posterior sampling methods for inverse problems. However, most of these approaches focus on Gaussian inverse problems, in which observations are generated through a deterministic forward operator corrupted by additive Gaussian noise. By contrast, Poisson inverse problems, where observations are discrete and Poisson distributed, remain comparatively underexplored in this literature. Building on our Poisson generative dynamics, we develop a natural framework for posterior sampling in Poisson inverse problems and derive several posterior sampling algorithms based on the proposed model. We evaluate our approach on realistic Poisson inverse problems and show that the resulting framework is well suited to this class of problems.

entry.title: Hierarchical Gaussian Processes for Survey Weighting: Local Equivalent Weights in Structured Populations

link.title: Hierarchical Gaussian Processes for Survey Weighting: Local Equivalent Weights in Structured Populations

entry.content: Regression-based survey weighting connects model-based population estimation with design-based inference through equivalent weights. For nonlinear models, equivalent weights can be defined locally through the sensitivity of a poststratified population estimator. However, conventional regression models may inadequately capture nonlinear relationships and complex interactions across sparse poststratification cells. We develop a survey-weighting framework based on hierarchical Gaussian process (HGP) regression, combining structured group-level effects with kernel-based smoothing to share information across related cells. We derive Gaussian posterior prediction formulas that exploit the structured covariance representation to reduce computational costs. We also establish a uniform convergence result for the posterior predictive mean under stated regularity conditions and construct local equivalent weights by matching the first-order sensitivity of a plug-in poststratified estimand to that of a weighted average of fitted response means, with both derivatives taken with respect to the latent mean-scale vector. Simulations show that HGP achieves lower population-weighted prediction error under nonparametric structure, whereas logistic regression performs well under correct parametric specification. Additional analyses examine sample size, frame coverage, subgroup prediction, and population-mean agreement. An application to the Future of Families and Child Wellbeing Study illustrates the method. Overall, this work extends local equivalent-weight construction to nonparametric modeling and provides a computational framework and conditional theoretical results for survey weighting in structured, sparse populations.

entry.title: Compound p-values for competition-based testing

link.title: Compound p-values for competition-based testing

entry.content: Standard competition-based multiple testing methods – such as the knockoff filter and the target-decoy procedure – are typically formulated as head-to-head competitions between a test unit and its assigned negative control unit. Motivated by real-world applications, which leverage any available negative controls, we study this competition-based framework in more intricate settings where competitions vary in size and structure. We propose new methods based on compound p-values – p-values that are superuniform only on aggregate – that enable powerful multiple testing with broader competition structures, via the Bonferroni and Benjamini-Hochberg procedures. The former provides exact familywise error rate control, whereas the latter may incur a false discovery rate inflation factor, for which we derive upper bounds across a range of settings. We showcase the performance of our general competition-based testing methodology through extensive simulations and real-data applications, including analyses of virtual spatial transcriptomics and CRISPR screen datasets that exhibit precisely the complex competition structures that motivate our methods.

entry.title: Testing Conditional Distribution Equality Using Generative Models

link.title: Testing Conditional Distribution Equality Using Generative Models

entry.content: Conditional distribution equality testing is a core problem with applications in causal inference, model diagnostics, and transfer learning. Existing methods often lose power when the conditioning variable is high-dimensional. We propose a new test that leverages generative models to compare conditional distributions using both observed data and synthetic samples. A sample-splitting and studentization scheme is introduced to control estimation error. Under the null, the test statistic is asymptotically normal, and we establish local power against contiguous alternatives. Our theory under the null and fixed alternative requires only consistency of the learned conditional distribution, allowing for a broad class of generative models. Empirical results demonstrate accurate size control and strong power in high-dimensional settings compared to representative kernel-based conditional and joint two-sample tests.

entry.title: On Complexity of Gaussian Sampling

link.title: On Complexity of Gaussian Sampling

entry.content: We study the number of exact matrix-vector queries needed to sample a centered $d$-dimensional Gaussian with condition number at most $\kappa$ to total variation error $\varepsilon$. The best known algorithm uses $O(\min{d,\sqrt{\kappa}\log(\frac{d}{\varepsilon})})$ queries, while the known lower bounds do not grow as $\varepsilon\to0$ and match this bound only for $\kappa\le d^{1/5-\delta}$ at constant accuracy. We introduce a construction based on a hidden determinant sign and prove a lower bound of $\Omega!\left(\min\left{d,\sqrt{\kappa}\log\left(1+\frac{d}{\sqrt{\kappa}\,\varepsilon}\right)\right}\right)$ uniformly for all $d\ge1$, $\kappa\ge4$, and $0 0$. We also extend a recent fixed-spectrum construction with a hidden eigenbasis from $\kappa=2$ to $2\le\kappa\le d^{1-\delta}$, for any fixed $\delta\in(0,1)$. This gives an $\Omega_\delta(\sqrt{\kappa}\log d)$ lower bound at constant accuracy that holds even when the spectrum of the precision matrix is known to the algorithm.

entry.title: Probabilistic AI models outperform numerical weather prediction models on record breaking heat extremes

link.title: Probabilistic AI models outperform numerical weather prediction models on record breaking heat extremes

entry.content: AI weather prediction (AIWP) models have emerged as a key complement to physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP) models, and now often outperform them on aggregate skill. Yet, several studies report that physics-based models still forecast extreme events better, in particular record-breaking extremes, based on the evaluation of deterministic forecasts. Here we evaluate heat extreme forecasts from probabilistic AIWP models over global land and show that they clearly outperform the ECMWF IFS ensemble, both raw and post-processed, including for record-breaking events, in all regions and at all lead times considered. AIWP models better forecast the occurrence and intensity of extremes, are better calibrated in the tail and miss fewer records. Station observations confirm these results. We argue that many reported AIWP limitations stem from unsuitable verification choices, specifically comparing deterministic forecasts that target different quantities. Instead, a fair evaluation of extremes necessitates probabilistic verification.

entry.title: The Physics Is the Network: Fast, Training-Free Neural Emulation

link.title: The Physics Is the Network: Fast, Training-Free Neural Emulation

entry.content: Neural emulation need not require learning a substitute for known physics. We investigate PolyNets that couple a continuous-time neural representation of polynomial dynamics with a simple recurrent network for discrete-time integration. When the governing coefficients are known, the resulting tensor graph requires no training and preserves the prescribed numerical scheme while enabling efficient hardware execution and parallel simulation. Using the one-dimensional Korteweg-de Vries equation, we compare PolyNet with CPU and GPU finite-difference Runge-Kutta solvers and three trained neural models: a state-map emulator, a physics-informed predictor, and a learned-tendency integrator. Analytical soliton solutions provide a reference for amplitude and phase errors across grid resolutions, 10^6 dispersively scaled time steps, ensembles of up to 10^4 trajectories, and varying initial amplitudes. PolyNet achieves accuracy comparable to the numerical solvers, including at amplitudes outside the learned models’ training conditions. It combines this fidelity with high GPU throughput, approximately constant over the tested resolution range, and favorable ensemble scaling.

entry.title: Noisy Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for doubly-intractable distributions

link.title: Noisy Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for doubly-intractable distributions

entry.content: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) has been progressively incorporated within the statistician’s toolbox as an alternative sampling method in settings when standard Metropolis-Hastings is inefficient. HMC generates a Markov chain on an augmented state space with transitions based on a deterministic differential flow derived from Hamiltonian mechanics. In practice, the evolution of Hamiltonian systems cannot be solved analytically, requiring numerical integration schemes. Under numerical integration, the resulting approximate solution no longer preserves the measure of the target distribution, therefore an accept-reject step is used to correct the bias. For doubly-intractable distributions – such as posterior distributions based on Gibbs random fields – HMC suffers from some computational difficulties: computation of gradients in the differential flow and computation of the accept-reject proposals poses difficulty. In this paper, we study the behaviour of HMC when these quantities are replaced by Monte Carlo estimates.

entry.title: Bayesian Nonparametric Thompson Sampling for Multi-Armed Bandits

link.title: Bayesian Nonparametric Thompson Sampling for Multi-Armed Bandits

entry.content: In stochastic multi-armed bandits, rewards are generated by an unknown distribution; the world’s reward uncertainty induces the exploration-exploitation trade-off. Thompson sampling (TS) addresses this trade-off elegantly, but requires knowing the reward model’s parametric form to sample from its posterior and compute per-arm expected rewards —which limits its applicability as it demands per-scenario model specification and hyperparameter tuning. We here adopt Bayesian nonparametric (BNP) mixture models to remove this requirement, extending TS to arbitrary reward distributions. We model each arm’s unknown reward distribution with an independent BNP Gaussian mixture, which can approximate any continuous reward density, and adapts its complexity to sequentially observed data. Embedding the BNP mixture model into TS yields Nonparametric TS, an algorithm that sequentially learns the reward model that best approximates the true, yet unknown, per-arm reward distribution, avoiding case-by-case model specification and hyperparameter tuning. We empirically demonstrate that ($i$) Nonparametric TS matches the regret performance of Oracle TS policies that know the true reward model; ($ii$) it favorably compares (in cumulative regret and volatility) to a suite of state-of-the-art alternatives across multimodal, outlier-contaminated, and non-exponential-family reward distributions; and ($iii$) its Bayesian nonparametric inference remains computationally practical and accurate for regret minimization.

entry.title: Decomposing Basketball Team Efficiency Using the Four Factors and Shapley Values

link.title: Decomposing Basketball Team Efficiency Using the Four Factors and Shapley Values

entry.content: Understanding how different aspects of basketball performance translate into overall team efficiency is central to analysis and strategy. This paper derives a mathematical expression that presents team offensive, defensive, and net ratings directly in terms of a team’s four factors and shooting percentages. The resulting formula captures the full nonlinear structure of how shooting, turnovers, rebounding, and free throws jointly interact to determine team efficiency. Using this relationship, we introduce a Shapley value-based framework that decomposes team net rating into a sum of contributions from individual factors. This way, different facets of the game are made commensurable. The decomposition requires only standard box-score statistics and a single parameter $\mu$, which represents the relative frequency of possession-ending free throws and remains constant for a given league and season. Consequently, it can be applied equally to individual games, full seasons, or league-wide trends. Moreover, it is immediately applicable to box-score statistics from any league or competition level by a simple change of reference point and the estimation of league- and season-specific parameter $\mu$. Empirical analyses using NBA data from 2000 to 2025 validate the offensive ratings produced by the formula against exact play-by-play data, showing a nearly perfect correlation ($r = 0.999$) and a low Mean Absolute Error of $0.188$ points per 100 possessions. These analyses further illustrate how the proposed framework can be used to quantify how teams achieve success in different ways or to explain the results of individual games.

link.title: Inference for Heterogeneous Graphical Models using Doubly High-Dimensional Linear-Mixed Models

entry.content: Inferring the structure of population-level functional connectivity networks from multi-subject functional magnetic resonance imaging data is essential for understanding the connectivity patterns underlying cognitive and behavioral functions. Graphical models provide a formal statistical framework for inferring the graph structure. However, the multi-level nature of functional magnetic resonance imaging data—where each level corresponds, for instance, to a subject—compromises the inferential validity of most existing methods. In this paper, we develop a valid inference framework for high-dimensional graphical models that accounts for cross-level heterogeneity. We introduce a neighborhood-based method to learn the graph structure and reframe the problem as that of inferring fixed effect parameters in a doubly high-dimensional linear mixed model. We then propose a LASSO-based estimator and a de-biased LASSO-based inference framework for these fixed effect parameters. We evaluate the performance of the proposed framework using benchmark simulation studies and apply it to descriptively compare graph structures between the functional connectivity networks of two predefined groups of subjects from the Human Connectome Project.

entry.title: Direction Preferring Confidence Intervals

link.title: Direction Preferring Confidence Intervals

entry.content: Confidence intervals (CIs) are fundamental in statistical analysis, providing interval estimates for unknown parameters. We introduce direction-preferring CIs that prioritize inference for parameters with a specific sign (e.g., positive sign). Unlike previous methods of constructing CIs, our intervals are based on the inversion of acceptance regions that differ for positive and negative parameters, to enhance the probability of determining the sign in the prespecified preferred direction while maintaining standard coverage. We apply our suggestion in the typical context that multiple parameters are considered, but only some of the constructed CIs are of interest, e.g., when CIs are reported only for the subset of parameters that are found to differ significantly from zero. This leads us to suggest direction-preferring CIs with false coverage rate (FCR) control, as well as conditional direction-preferring CIs that adjust for selection by conditioning on the selection event. We compare the two selection adjustment methods in theory and using numerical experiments. The procedures we develop are useful for inference on secondary outcomes in medical applications, a setting we highlight through two motivating examples.

entry.title: Testing for an Explosive Bubble using High-Frequency Volatility

link.title: Testing for an Explosive Bubble using High-Frequency Volatility

entry.content: Based on a continuous-time stochastic volatility model with a linear drift, we develop a test for explosive behavior in financial asset prices at a low frequency when prices are sampled at a higher frequency. The test exploits the volatility information in the high-frequency data. The method consists of devolatizing log-asset price increments with realized volatility measures and performing a supremum-type recursive Dickey-Fuller test on the devolatized sample. The proposed test has a nuisance-parameter-free asymptotic distribution and is easy to implement. We study the size and power properties of the test in Monte Carlo simulations. A real-time date-stamping strategy based on the devolatized sample is proposed for the origination and conclusion dates of the explosive regime. Conditions under which the real-time date-stamping strategy is consistent are established. The test and the date-stamping strategy are applied to study explosive behavior in cryptocurrency and stock markets.

entry.title: Watermarking Continuous Tabular Data Generation

link.title: Watermarking Continuous Tabular Data Generation

entry.content: In this paper, we introduce a simple yet effective tabular data watermarking mechanism with statistical guarantees. We show theoretically that the proposed watermark can be effectively detected, while faithfully preserving the data fidelity, and also demonstrates appealing robustness against additive noise attack. The general idea is to achieve the watermarking through a strategic embedding based on simple data binning. Specifically, it divides the feature’s value range into finely segmented intervals and embeds watermarks into selected ``green list” intervals. To detect the watermarks, we develop a principled statistical hypothesis-testing framework with minimal assumptions: it remains valid as long as the underlying data distribution has a continuous density function. The watermarking efficacy is demonstrated through rigorous theoretical analysis and empirical validation, highlighting its utility in enhancing the security of synthetic and real-world datasets.

entry.title: Exploring Exchangeability within Permutation Inference: Implications for Statistics and Data Science Educators

link.title: Exploring Exchangeability within Permutation Inference: Implications for Statistics and Data Science Educators

entry.content: Permutation tests are a powerful and flexible approach to inference via resampling. As computational methods become more ubiquitous in the statistics curriculum, use of permutation tests has become more tractable. At the heart of the permutation approach is the exchangeability condition, which determines the appropriate null sampling distribution. We explore the exchangeability condition in the context of permutation tests, including settings where the exchangeability condition is not tenable. Our examples include two-sample comparisons of means, clustered designs, multiple linear regression, and two-sample comparisons of correlation. The different exchangeability challenges in each example allow further exploration of the definition and importance of the exchangeability requirement for permutation testing. We believe that understanding the exchangeability condition and how it relates to the null hypothesis gives students the skills to work effectively with permutation tests in more complicated modeling settings and to further their understanding of statistical inference. We close with pedagogical recommendations for instructors who wish to incorporate permutation inference into their curriculum as a means to increase student understanding of resampling-based inference.

link.title: Bootstrap Adaptive Lasso Solution Path Unit Root Tests

entry.content: We propose sieve wild bootstrap analogues to the adaptive Lasso solution path unit root tests of Arnold and Reinschl"ussel (2024) arXiv:2404.06205 to improve finite sample properties and extend their applicability to a generalised framework, allowing for non-stationary volatility. entry.title: Generative Conformal Prediction with Optimized Coverage Allocation

link.title: Generative Conformal Prediction with Optimized Coverage Allocation

entry.content: Conformal prediction provides model-agnostic uncertainty quantification with guaranteed coverage, but conventional methods often yield overly conservative uncertainty sets, particularly in multimodal or heterogeneous settings. This inefficiency arises from two sources: (i) limited expressiveness of the predictive model and (ii) simplistic nonconformity score design. Most existing approaches advance only one of these axes, leaving the other underexplored. We propose generative conformal prediction with Optimized Ranking and Coverage Allocation (ORCA), a three-stage framework that advances both aspects jointly. ORCA leverages generative models to capture the full conditional distribution and introduces a rank-dependent optimization procedure that adaptively allocates coverage for efficiency while maintaining validity. We cast this coverage allocation as an optimization problem, derive an exact mixed-integer linear programming formulation, and show that the solution converges asymptotically to the oracle density-level set. Across synthetic, semi-synthetic, and real datasets, ORCA produces substantially more efficient uncertainty sets than state-of-the-art baselines, demonstrating robust gains in scenarios where conventional conformal prediction methods fail.

entry.title: Simulations for estimation of random effects and overall effect in three-level meta-analysis of standardized mean differences using constant and inverse-variance weights

link.title: Simulations for estimation of random effects and overall effect in three-level meta-analysis of standardized mean differences using constant and inverse-variance weights

entry.content: We consider a three-level meta-analysis of standardized mean differences. The standard method of estimation uses inverse-variance weights and REML/PL estimation of variance components for the random effects. We introduce new moment-based point and interval estimators for the two variance components and related estimators of the overall mean. Similar to traditional analysis of variance, our method is based on two conditional $Q$ statistics with effective-sample-size weights. entry.title: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Monte Carlo Simulations in A/B Testing

link.title: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Monte Carlo Simulations in A/B Testing

entry.content: This paper examines the use of Monte Carlo simulations to understand statistical concepts in A/B testing and Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs). We discuss the applicability of simulations in understanding false positive rates and estimating statistical power, implementing variance reduction techniques and examining the effects of early stopping. By comparing frequentist and Bayesian approaches, we illustrate how simulations can clarify the relationship between p-values and posterior probabilities, and the validity of such approximations. The study also references how Monte Carlo simulations can be used to understand network effects in RCTs on social networks. Our findings show that Monte Carlo simulations are an effective tool for experimenters to deepen their understanding and ensure their results are statistically valid and practically meaningful.

link.title: WMAP: An R Package for Causal Meta-Analysis by Integrating Multiple Observational Studies

entry.content: Integrating multiple observational studies for meta-analysis has sparked much interest. The presented R package WMAP (Weighted Meta-Analysis with Pseudo-Populations) (Guha et al., 2026) addresses a critical gap in the implementation of integrative weighting approaches for multiple observational studies and causal inferences about various groups of subjects, such as disease subtypes. The package features three weighting approaches, each representing a special case of the unified weighting framework introduced by Guha and Li (2024), which includes an extension of inverse probability weights for data integration settings. It performs meta-analysis on user-inputted datasets as follows: (i) it first estimates the propensity scores for study-group combinations, calculates subject balancing weights, and determines the effective sample size (ESS) for a user-specified weighting method; and (ii) it then estimates various features of multiple counterfactual group outcomes, such as group medians and differences in group means for the mRNA expression of eight genes. Additionally, bootstrap variability estimates are provided. Among the implemented weighting methods, we highlight the FLEXible, Optimized, and Realistic (FLEXOR) method, which is specifically designed to maximize the ESS within the unified framework. The use of the software is illustrated through simulations and a multi-site breast cancer case study based on a simulated dataset modeled after real TCGA data from seven medical centers.

entry.title: Targeted Data Fusion for Region-Specific Survival Effects in the AMP HIV Prevention Trials

link.title: Targeted Data Fusion for Region-Specific Survival Effects in the AMP HIV Prevention Trials

entry.content: The Antibody Mediated Prevention (AMP) trials opened a new scientific frontier by showing that passively administered monoclonal broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) could prevent HIV-1 acquisition. The trials enrolled 4,611 participants across four epidemiologically distinct regions, with 174 HIV-1 diagnoses observed during follow-up. Regional heterogeneity in treatment efficacy, together with privacy and regulatory limits on central data pooling, calls for methods that borrow strength across regions without sharing individual-level data. To estimate region- and treatment-specific survival curves under distributional heterogeneity, we develop a federated learning approach that combines site-specific estimators via an L1-regularized criterion that downweights data sources not aligned with the target. We further extend the framework to a general class of causal contrasts, including the survival difference, survival ratio, and restricted mean survival time difference. In the AMP analysis, for example, the standard error of the day-148 survival difference decreased from 0.007 using the target-only estimator to 0.004 using the federated estimator. For women in South Africa, the region-specific analyses provided no strong evidence of an overall VRC01 benefit, consistent with the primary AMP findings. Overall, the proposed approach provides region-adaptive inference with improved precision without sharing individual-level data, while preserving estimation of region-specific treatment effects under cross-region heterogeneity.

entry.title: Stein’s unbiased risk estimate and Hyvärinen’s score matching

link.title: Stein’s unbiased risk estimate and Hyvärinen’s score matching

entry.content: Given a collection of observed signals corrupted with Gaussian noise, how can we learn to optimally denoise them? This fundamental problem arises in both empirical Bayes and generative modeling. In empirical Bayes, the predominant approach is via nonparametric maximum likelihood estimation (NPMLE), while in generative modeling, score matching (SM) methods have proven very successful. In our setting, Hyv"arinen’s implicit SM is equivalent to another classical idea from statistics—Stein’s Unbiased Risk Estimate (SURE). Revisiting SURE minimization, we establish, for the first time, that SURE achieves nearly parametric rates of convergence of the regret in the classical empirical Bayes setting with homoscedastic noise. We also prove that SURE-training can achieve fast rates of convergence to the oracle denoiser in a commonly studied misspecified model. We show how to practically implement our method in settings involving heteroscedasticity and side-information, such as in an application to the estimation of economic mobility in the Opportunity Atlas. Our empirical results demonstrate the superior performance of SURE-training over NPMLE under misspecification. Collectively, our findings advance SURE/SM as a strong alternative to the NPMLE for empirical Bayes problems in both theory and practice.

entry.title: Sublinear Algorithms for Wasserstein and Total Variation Distances: Applications to Fairness and Privacy Auditing

link.title: Sublinear Algorithms for Wasserstein and Total Variation Distances: Applications to Fairness and Privacy Auditing

entry.content: Resource-efficiently computing representations of probability distributions and the distances between them while only having access to the samples is a fundamental and useful problem across mathematical sciences. In this paper, we propose a generic framework to learn the probability and cumulative distribution functions (PDFs and CDFs) of a sub-Weibull, i.e. almost any light- or heavy-tailed, distribution while the samples from it arrive in a stream. The idea is to reduce these problems into estimating the frequency of an appropriately chosen subset of the support of a properly discretised distribution. We leverage this reduction to compute mergeable summaries of distributions from the stream of samples while requiring only sublinear space relative to the number of observed samples. This allows us to estimate Wasserstein and Total Variation (TV) distances between any two distributions while samples arrive in streams and from multiple sources. Our algorithms significantly improves on the existing methods for distance estimation incurring super-linear time and linear space complexities, and further extend the mergeable summaries framework to continuous distributions with possibly infinite support. Our results are tight with respect to the existing lower bounds for bounded discrete distributions. In addition, we leverage our proposed estimators of Wasserstein and TV distances to tightly audit the fairness and privacy of algorithms. We empirically demonstrate the efficiency of proposed algorithms across synthetic and real-world datasets.

entry.content: We introduce a Bayesian framework for indirect local clustering of functional data, leveraging B-spline basis expansions and a novel dependent random partition model. By exploiting the local support properties of B-splines, our approach allows partially coincident functional behaviors, achieved when shared basis coefficients span sufficiently contiguous regions. This is accomplished through a cutting-edge dependent random partition model that enforces semi-Markovian dependence across a sequence of partitions. By matching the degree of the B-spline basis with the semi-Markovian dependence structure, the proposed model serves as a highly flexible prior, enabling efficient modeling of localized features in functional data. Furthermore, we extend the utility of the dependent random partition model beyond functional data, demonstrating its applicability to a broad class of problems where sequences of dependent partitions are central, and standard Markovian assumptions prove overly restrictive. Empirical illustrations, including analyses of simulated data and tide level measurements from the Venice Lagoon, showcase the effectiveness and versatility of the proposed methodology.

entry.title: A longitudinal Bayesian framework for estimating causal dose-response relationships

link.title: A longitudinal Bayesian framework for estimating causal dose-response relationships

entry.content: Existing causal methods for time-varying exposure and time-varying confounding focus on estimating the average causal effect of a time-varying binary treatment on an end-of-study outcome, offering limited tools for characterizing marginal causal dose-response relationships under continuous exposures. We propose a scalable, nonparametric Bayesian framework for estimating marginal longitudinal causal dose-response functions with repeated outcome measurements. Our approach targets the average potential outcome at any fixed dose level and accommodates time-varying confounding through the generalized propensity score. The proposed approach embeds a Dirichlet process specification within a generalized estimating equations structure, capturing temporal correlation while making minimal assumptions about the functional form of the continuous exposure. We apply the proposed methods to monthly metro ridership and COVID-19 case data from major international cities, identifying causal relationships and the dose-response patterns between higher ridership and increased case counts.

entry.title: Dependent Dirichlet processes via thinning

link.title: Dependent Dirichlet processes via thinning

entry.content: When analyzing data from multiple sources, it is often convenient to strike a careful balance between two goals: capturing the heterogeneity of the samples and sharing information across them. We introduce a novel framework to model a collection of samples using dependent Dirichlet processes constructed through a thinning mechanism. The proposed approach modifies the stick-breaking representation of the Dirichlet process by thinning, that is, setting equal to zero a random subset of the beta random variables used in the original construction. This results in a collection of dependent random distributions that exhibit both shared and unique atoms, with the shared ones assigned distinct weights in each distribution. The generality of the construction allows expressing a wide variety of dependence structures among the elements of the generated random vectors. Moreover, its simplicity facilitates the characterization of several theoretical properties and the derivation of efficient computational methods for posterior inference. A simulation study illustrates how a modeling approach based on the proposed process reduces uncertainty in group-specific inferences while preventing excessive borrowing of information when the data indicate it is unnecessary. This added flexibility improves the accuracy of posterior inference, outperforming related state-of-the-art models. An application to the Collaborative Perinatal Project data highlights the model’s capability to estimate group-specific densities and uncover a meaningful partition of the observations, both within and across samples, providing valuable insights into the underlying data structure.

link.title: Learning Smooth Populations of Parameters with Trial Heterogeneity

entry.content: We consider the classical problem of estimating the mixing distribution of binomial mixtures, but under trial heterogeneity and smoothness. This problem has been studied extensively when the trial parameter is homogeneous, but not under the more general scenario of heterogeneous trials, and only within a low smoothness regime, where the resulting rates are slow. Under the assumption that the density is s-smooth, we derive fast error rates for the kernel density estimator under trial heterogeneity that depend on the harmonic mean of the trials. Importantly, even when reduced to the homogeneous case, our result improves on the state-of-the-art rate of Ye and Bickel (2021). We also study nonparametric estimation of the difference between two densities, which can be smoother than the individual densities, in both i.i.d. and binomial-mixture settings. Our work is motivated by an application in criminal justice: comparing conviction rates of indigent representation in Pennsylvania. We find that the estimated conviction rates for appointed counsel (court-appointed private attorneys) are generally higher than those for public defenders, potentially due to a confounding factor: appointed counsel are more likely to take on severe cases.

entry.title: Fluoride Varnish in a Changing Preventive Environment: A Reanalysis and Temporal Meta-Regression of Historical and Contemporary Trials

link.title: Fluoride Varnish in a Changing Preventive Environment: A Reanalysis and Temporal Meta-Regression of Historical and Contemporary Trials

entry.content: Historical trials of fluoride varnish reported large reductions in dental caries, but contemporary trials are often conducted against more intensive background prevention, so the incremental effect may be smaller. For positive continuous outcomes, we modeled the log ratio of treatment to control means and report the prevented fraction, $\mathrm{PF}=1-\exp(y)$. A nine-trial historical dataset was reanalyzed using REML with Hartung–Knapp inference, Bayesian hierarchical models, and sensitivity analyses; completeness was checked against all 13 Cochrane permanent-surface trials. Temporal change was examined in a 14-study dataset combining nine historical and five contemporary trials, with time specifications compared by AICc. The historical pooled PF was $39.7\%$ (95% CI $18.0\%$ to $55.6\%$), with a much wider 95% prediction interval ($-26.5\%$ to $71.2\%$). Expanding to 13 Cochrane trials barely changed the direct estimate ($0.439$ to $0.435$). The calendar coefficient was $0.0986$ log-ratio units per decade (95% CI $-0.0445$ to $0.2417$), with fitted PF declining from $34.8%$ in 2005 to $20.6%$ in 2025. A Bayesian model gave a similar slope (posterior median $0.091$; 95% CrI $-0.036$ to $0.231$). The intercept-only model had the lowest AICc, though the linear-time model was within two units. Adjusting for background prevention reduced the slope to $0.057$ per decade. The historical average effect is stable across modeling choices, whereas prediction for a new setting is much less certain. Contemporary evidence is compatible with attenuation of the incremental varnish effect but does not require a temporal moderator; the pattern is consistent with a changing treatment contrast rather than weakened biological action.

entry.title: An Infinite BART model

link.title: An Infinite BART model

entry.content: Bayesian additive regression trees (BART) is a popular Bayesian ensemble model used in regression and classification analysis. Under this modeling framework, the regression function is approximated by an ensemble of decision trees, interpreted as weak learners. In this work, we propose a generalization of the BART model that has two main features: first, it automatically selects the number of decision trees using the given data; second, the model allows clusters of observations to have different regression functions since each data point can only use a selection of weak learners, instead of all of them. This model generalization is accomplished by including a binary weight matrix in the conditional distribution of the response variable, which activates only a specific subset of decision trees for each observation. Such a matrix is endowed with an Indian Buffet process prior, and sampled within the MCMC sampler, together with the other BART parameters. We then compare the Infinite BART model with the classic one on simulated and real datasets. Specifically, we provide examples illustrating variable importance, partial dependence and causal estimation.

entry.title: Assumption-Lean Differential Variance Inference for Heterogeneous Treatment Effect Detection

link.title: Assumption-Lean Differential Variance Inference for Heterogeneous Treatment Effect Detection

entry.content: The conditional average treatment effect (CATE) is frequently estimated in clinical studies to refute a homogeneous treatment effect hypothesis. Under this regime, all patients making up the population experience identical benefit from a given treatment relative to a comparator. Uncovering heterogeneous treatment effects through inference about the CATE, however, requires that covariates truly modifying the treatment effect be reliably collected at baseline. CATE-based techniques will necessarily fail to detect violations when effect modifiers are omitted from the data due to, for example, resource constraints. Severe measurement error has a similar impact. Clinical decision makers can be misled as a result. To address these limitations, we prove that a practical homogeneous treatment effect hypothesis can be gauged through inference about contrasts of the potential outcomes’ variances even when effect modifiers are missing from the data. We derive causal machine learning estimators of these contrasts and study their asymptotic properties. We establish that these estimators are doubly robust and asymptotically linear under mild conditions, permitting formal hypothesis testing about treatment effect heterogeneity. Numerical experiments demonstrate that these estimators’ asymptotic guarantees are approximately achieved in finite-sample randomized and observational study data alike. These inference procedures are then used to detect heterogeneous treatment effects in the re-analysis of randomized controlled trials investigating targeted temperature management in cardiac arrest patients.

entry.title: Detecting Impact of the Great Recession on Macroeconomic Indicators

link.title: Detecting Impact of the Great Recession on Macroeconomic Indicators

entry.content: We study structural changes in multivariate time series by estimating and comparing stationary graphs of macroeconomic time series before and after an economic crisis, such as the Great Recession. Building on a latent time series framework called Orthogonally-rotated Univariate Time-series (OUT), we propose a shared-parameter framework-the spOUT autoregressive model (spOUTAR)-that jointly models two related multivariate time series and enables coherent Bayesian estimation of their corresponding stationary precision matrices. This framework provides a principled mechanism for detecting and quantifying which conditional relationships among the variables changed or formed following the crisis. Specifically, we study the impact of the Great Recession (December 2007-June 2009) that substantially disrupted global and national economies, prompting long-lasting shifts in macroeconomic indicators and their interrelationships. While many studies document its economic consequences, less is known about how the underlying conditional dependency structure among economic variables changed as economies moved from pre-crisis stability through the shock and back to normalcy. Using the proposed approach to analyze U.S. and OECD macroeconomic data, we demonstrate that spOUTAR effectively captures recession-induced changes in stationary graphical structure, offering a flexible and interpretable tool for studying structural shifts in economic systems.

entry.title: Nonparametric Stochastic Subspaces via the Bootstrap Method for Characterizing Model Error

link.title: Nonparametric Stochastic Subspaces via the Bootstrap Method for Characterizing Model Error

entry.content: Reliable forward uncertainty quantification in engineering requires methods that account for aleatory and epistemic uncertainties. In many applications, epistemic effects arising from uncertain parameters and model form dominate prediction error and strongly influence engineering decisions. Because distinguishing and representing each source separately is often infeasible, their combined effect is typically analyzed using a unified model-error framework. Model error directly affects model credibility and predictive reliability; yet its characterization remains challenging. To address this need, we introduce a bootstrap-based stochastic subspace model for characterizing model error in the stochastic reduced-order modeling framework. Given a snapshot matrix of state vectors, the method leverages the empirical data distribution to induce a sampling distribution over principal subspaces for reduced order modeling. The resulting stochastic model enables improved characterization of model error in computational mechanics compared with existing approaches. The method offers several advantages: (1) it is assumption-free and leverages the empirical data distribution; (2) it enforces linear constraints (such as boundary conditions) by construction; (3) it requires only one hyperparameter, significantly simplifying the training process; and (4) its algorithm is straightforward to implement. We evaluate the method’s performance against existing approaches using numerical examples in computational mechanics and structural dynamics.

entry.title: Fully Bayesian Spectral Clustering and Benchmarking with Uncertainty Quantification for Small Area Estimation

link.title: Fully Bayesian Spectral Clustering and Benchmarking with Uncertainty Quantification for Small Area Estimation

entry.content: In this work, inspired by machine learning techniques, we propose a new Bayesian model for Small Area Estimation (SAE), the Fay-Herriot model with Spectral Clustering (FH-SC). Unlike traditional approaches, clustering in FH-SC is based on spectral clustering algorithms that utilize external covariates, rather than geographical or administrative criteria. A major advantage of the FH-SC model is its flexibility in integrating existing SAE approaches, with or without clustering random effects. To enable benchmarking, we leverage the theoretical framework of posterior projections for constrained Bayesian inference and derive closed form expressions for the new Rao-Blackwell (RB) estimators of the posterior mean under the FH-SC model. Additionally, we introduce a novel measure of uncertainty for the benchmarked estimator, the Conditional Posterior Mean Square Error (CPMSE), which is generalizable to other Bayesian SAE estimators. We conduct model-based and data-based simulation studies to evaluate the frequentist properties of the CPMSE. The proposed methodology is motivated by a real case study involving the estimation of the proportion of households with internet access in the municipalities of Colombia. Finally, we also illustrate the advantages of FH-SC over existing Bayesian and frequentist approaches through our case study.

entry.title: Sampling from multimodal distributions with warm starts: Non-asymptotic bounds for the Reweighted Annealed Leap-Point Sampler

link.title: Sampling from multimodal distributions with warm starts: Non-asymptotic bounds for the Reweighted Annealed Leap-Point Sampler

entry.content: Sampling from multimodal distributions is a central challenge in Bayesian inference and machine learning. In light of hardness results for sampling – classical MCMC methods, even with tempering, can suffer from exponential mixing times – a natural question is how to leverage additional information, such as a warm start point for each mode, to enable faster mixing across modes. To address this, we introduce Reweighted ALPS (Re-ALPS), a modified version of the Annealed Leap-Point Sampler (ALPS) that dispenses with the Gaussian approximation assumption. We prove the first polynomial-time bound that works in a general setting, under a natural assumption that each component contains significant mass relative to the others when tilted towards the corresponding warm start point. Similarly to ALPS, we define distributions tilted towards a mixture centered at the warm start points, and at the coldest level, use teleportation between warm start points to enable efficient mixing across modes. In contrast to ALPS, our method does not require Hessian information at the modes, but instead estimates component partition functions via Monte Carlo. This additional estimation step is crucial in allowing the algorithm to handle target distributions with more complex geometries besides approximate Gaussian. For the proof, we show convergence results for Markov processes when only part of the stationary distribution is well-mixing and estimation for partition functions for individual components of a mixture.

entry.title: Learned Hemodynamic Coupling Inference in Resting-State Functional MRI

link.title: Learned Hemodynamic Coupling Inference in Resting-State Functional MRI

entry.content: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) provides an indirect measurement of neuronal activity via hemodynamic responses that vary across brain regions and individuals. Ignoring this hemodynamic variability can bias downstream connectivity estimates. Furthermore, the hemodynamic parameters themselves may serve as important imaging biomarkers. Estimating spatially varying hemodynamics from resting-state fMRI (rsfMRI) is therefore an important but challenging blind inverse problem, since both the latent neural activity and the hemodynamic coupling are unknown. In this work, we propose a methodology for inferring hemodynamic coupling on the cortical surface from rsfMRI. Our approach avoids the highly unstable joint recovery of neural activity and hemodynamics by marginalizing out the latent neural signal and basing inference on the resulting marginal likelihood. To enable scalable, high-resolution estimation, we employ a deep neural network combined with conditional normalizing flows to accurately approximate this intractable marginal likelihood, while enforcing spatial coherence through priors defined on the cortical surface that admit sparse representations. Uncertainty in the hemodynamic estimates is quantified via a double-bootstrap procedure. The proposed approach is extensively validated using synthetic data and real fMRI datasets, demonstrating clear improvements over current methods for hemodynamic estimation and downstream connectivity reproducibility.

entry.title: Consistent and scalable detection and comparison of spatial patterns

link.title: Consistent and scalable detection and comparison of spatial patterns

entry.content: Spatial omics maps molecular features within tissues to study their organization across biological contexts, including disease and development. Interpreting these maps requires distinguishing patterns from noise and comparing them across samples. Yet pattern detection remains unresolved, and comparisons based on regional summaries lose spatial detail. Here we show that spatial frequency provides a common basis for detecting and comparing these patterns. Our framework, SONIC, unifies spatial detection tests through a common quadratic form, establishes conditions for reliable detection and explains how kernel choice determines sensitivity to different spatial patterns. It also separates changes in spatial organization from changes in overall abundance without aligning tissues. Fast, memory-efficient algorithms make detection and comparison practical across large datasets. Applying SONIC, we identify plaque-associated responses in Alzheimer’s disease and differences in the spatial expression of blood-clotting genes between glioma subtypes. We further construct a gene-centric atlas that traces changes in spatial expression through mouse and human embryogenesis and supports retrieval of related patterns across species. These results extend spatial analysis from identifying individual patterns to following their changes across anatomically different tissues. Together, SONIC establishes a shared language for integrating molecular maps across studies and technologies.

entry.title: Prior Smoothing for Multivariate Disease Mapping Models

link.title: Prior Smoothing for Multivariate Disease Mapping Models

entry.content: To date, we have seen the emergence of a large literature on multivariate disease mapping. That is, incidence of (or mortality from) multiple diseases is recorded at the scale of areal units where incidence (mortality) across the diseases is expected to manifest dependence. The modeling involves a hierarchical structure: a Poisson model for disease counts (conditioning on the rates) at the first stage, and a specification of a function of the rates using spatial random effects at the second stage. These random effects are specified as a prior and introduce spatial smoothing to the rate (or risk) estimates. What we see in the literature is the amount of smoothing induced under a given prior across areal units compared with the observed/empirical risks. Our contribution here extends previous research on smoothing in univariate areal data models. Specifically, for three different choices of multivariate prior, we investigate both within prior smoothing according to hyperparameters and across prior smoothing. Its benefit to the user is to illuminate the expected nature of departure from perfect fit associated with these priors, providing measures of their smoothing behavior not captured by conventional measures of predictive performance. We propose both theoretical and empirical metrics for our investigation and illustrate with both simulated and real data.

link.title: Design-based theory for covariate adjustment in generalized pairwise comparisons

entry.content: Generalized pairwise comparisons summarize treatment effects in randomized experiments with ordinal, multivariate, or prioritized outcomes. We study optimal covariate adjustment under complete randomization, with potential outcomes and covariates fixed and treatment assignment as the sole source of randomness. We derive the exact randomization variance of the unadjusted estimator and characterize linear calibration adjustments using the between-arm difference in covariate means. The asymptotic variance is a strictly convex quadratic in the adjustment coefficient, yielding a closed-form optimum. The resulting estimator is asymptotically no less efficient than the unadjusted estimator, with an explicit precision gain that clarifies which covariates improve precision. However, natural pair-level and single-arm least squares adjustments generally use weights that differ from the allocation-dependent optimum and can substantially reduce efficiency. We also propose a within-arm variance estimator for asymptotically conservative inference, whose conservatism arises from unidentifiable joint variation in a unit’s two potential scores, and show that residualizing each arm on its own projection coefficient saves the discrepancy that governs the efficiency loss of conventional adjustments. In the special case where the comparison function is the outcome difference, our proposed covariate-adjusted estimator is first-order equivalent to the fully interacted regression adjustment of Lin (Ann. Appl. Stat., 2013, 7, 295-318).
